title: Mathlib Imports for Analysis
content: Imports integer and real number basics, the Irrational predicate, filter-based limits for the lim inf condition, infinite sums (tsum) for defining the series, and general tactics. The formalization bridges number theory (irrationality) with analysis (convergence of infinite sums).
mathContext: We use $\texttt{Irrational}$ from Mathlib for the irrationality predicate, $\texttt{Filter.liminf}$ for the growth condition $\liminf a_n^{1/2^n} > 1$, and $\texttt{tsum}$ for $\sum_{n=0}^\infty$.

title: Growth Condition: lim inf aₙ^{1/2ⁿ} > 1
content: The growth condition requires the lim inf of the doubly-exponential root of the sequence to exceed 1. Concretely, this means there exists alpha > 1 such that aₙ is at least alpha^{2ⁿ} for infinitely many n—the sequence grows at least as fast as a tower of exponentials. This is much weaker than the quadratic recurrence aₙ₊₁ ≥ C·aₙ² for which irrationality is known, making the gap between the two conditions the central difficulty.
mathContext:
$$\liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n^{1/2^n} > 1 \iff \exists\, \alpha > 1 : a_n \geq \alpha^{2^n} \text{ eventually}$$
This implies $a_n$ grows at least doubly exponentially: $a_n \geq \alpha^{2^n}$.

title: The Erdős Reciprocal Product Series
content: The series Σ 1/(aₙ·aₙ₊₁) sums reciprocals of consecutive products. This resembles a telescoping series—for Sylvester-type sequences where aₙ₊₁ = aₙ² - aₙ + 1, partial fractions give 1/(aₙ·aₙ₊₁) = 1/(aₙ - 1) - 1/(aₙ₊₁ - 1), connecting to known irrationals. The series converges rapidly under the growth condition.

title: Erdős Problem #1051: Universal Irrationality
content: The central conjecture: for every strictly increasing integer sequence satisfying the growth condition, the reciprocal product series is irrational. This is a universal statement—it must hold for all such sequences, not just specific examples. The difficulty lies in the diversity of sequences satisfying the growth condition, which includes sequences growing much slower than the quadratic recurrence for which irrationality is known.

title: Rapid Growth Case (Erdős, 1988)
content: Erdős (1988) proved irrationality when the sequence satisfies the quadratic recurrence aₙ₊₁ ≥ C·aₙ² for some constant C > 0. Under this stronger growth condition, the partial sums approximate the total sum so rapidly that rational approximation is impossible. The proof uses the theory of lacunary series and continued fraction-type arguments. The gap between this quadratic growth and the general growth condition is exactly what remains open.
mathContext: If $\exists\, C > 0 : a_{n+1} \geq C \cdot a_n^2$ for all $n$, then $\sum 1/(a_n a_{n+1}) \notin \mathbb{Q}$. Note: $a_{n+1} \geq C a_n^2$ implies $a_n \geq C^{2^n - 1} a_0^{2^n}$, which is stronger than $\liminf a_n^{1/2^n} > 1$.

title: Series Convergence Under Growth Condition
content: Under the growth condition, the series converges absolutely. Since aₙ grows at least doubly exponentially, the terms 1/(aₙ·aₙ₊₁) decay faster than any geometric series. Summability is the prerequisite for asking about irrationality.
mathContext: If $\liminf a_n^{1/2^n} > 1$, then $\sum |1/(a_n a_{n+1})|$ converges. The terms satisfy $1/(a_n a_{n+1}) \leq \alpha^{-3 \cdot 2^n}$ for $\alpha > 1$.

title: Positivity of the Series
content: When all terms aₙ are positive, each summand 1/(aₙ·aₙ₊₁) is positive, so the series sum is positive. This ensures the series doesn't trivially equal zero and is a meaningful quantity to study for irrationality.

title: Simple Reciprocal Series
content: The simpler series Σ 1/aₙ (without the consecutive product structure) is also conjectured irrational under the same growth condition. This is a related but distinct question—the product series Σ 1/(aₙ·aₙ₊₁) has an additional telescoping structure that might make it either easier or harder to analyze.
mathContext:
$$T(a) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{a_n}$$
Compare with $S(a) = \sum 1/(a_n a_{n+1})$. Note $1/a_n \geq 1/(a_n a_{n+1})$ when $a_{n+1} \geq 1$.

title: Simple Series Irrationality Conjecture
content: Erdős also asked whether Σ 1/aₙ is irrational under the same growth condition. This companion problem has similar status—known for rapid growth sequences but open in general. The two questions may be related but neither implies the other in an obvious way.

title: Sylvester–Fibonacci Example
content: The Sylvester sequence (defined by s₁ = 2, sₙ₊₁ = sₙ(sₙ − 1) + 1) and Fibonacci-type subsequences aₙ = F_{2ⁿ} provide concrete examples where the growth condition holds and the series is provably irrational. For Sylvester's sequence, the identity Σ 1/(sₙ − 1) = 1 gives a telescoping structure. These examples show the conjecture holds in important special cases.
mathContext: The Sylvester sequence: $s_1 = 2$, $s_{n+1} = s_n^2 - s_n + 1$. Satisfies $s_{n+1} \approx s_n^2$, so $\liminf s_n^{1/2^n} = 2 > 1$. The identity $\sum_{n=1}^{N} 1/(s_n - 1) = 1 - 1/\prod_{k=1}^{N} (s_k - 1)$ gives a telescoping structure.
